1:
The added name in the title sets five of them arguing. John Calvin sees no reason why the psalm should not be Solomon’s, and rejects the Jewish reading that takes the prefixed letter as meaning for rather than of, since such a title in all cases designates the author, so that to devise a new sense for it is needless and absurd. Keil and Delitzsch think the name added only because the second verse alludes to the name given to Solomon at his birth and to the wisdom and riches granted him in the dream, and because the psalm has the form of a proverb-song; they add that an early expositor already observed how much better the psalm suits the days of the rebuilding under Zerubbabel. Adam Clarke lists the versions that carry the name and those that carry none, and judges it most likely composed for the second temple under Nehemiah by some prophet of that time. Matthew Henry keeps the name but reverses the direction, making it a father’s instruction to a son cried up for wisdom and therefore apt to lean on his own forecast. Augustine of Hippo takes the difficulty to be moral rather than historical: Solomon fell, yet the good delivered through him is to be attributed to God and the man’s sin to the man, for Adam fell in Paradise and an angel fell from heaven, and no hope is to be placed in any among men.

What house is meant is less disputed than what the saying forbids. Charles Ellicott says flatly that it is a house, any house, and not the temple, the thought being general. John Calvin widens both nouns, taking house for the whole domestic order and government of a family and city for the general state of the commonwealth. Adam Clarke notes that the words for son, for daughter and for house all come from one root meaning to build, since sons and daughters constitute a family as truly as stones and timber constitute a building. John Calvin then guards the saying from misuse: it does not reject labour or enterprise or counsel, for it is a praiseworthy virtue to discharge the duties of our office diligently, and it is not the will of the Lord that we should be like blocks of wood or keep our arms folded. John Gill and C.H. Spurgeon both instance the builders of Babel, and Matthew Henry adds that if the foundations are laid in oppression God certainly does not build there.

The last clause is the crux. Charles Ellicott lays out both readings at length: the word for sleep may be the direct object of the verb, as the old versions took it, so that sleep itself is the gift; or it may stand adverbially, so that what others toil for from morning to night God gives his beloved while they sleep. That the second suits the context best there can, he says, be no question, and he supports it with a Greek proverb that the net catches while the fisher sleeps and a German one that God bestows his gifts during the night. Yet old association pleads for the other rendering, equally true and equally beautiful, since the ancients called sleep the most grateful of known gifts and made it a god. John Wesley takes the adverbial sense, that God gives freely without the immoderate toiling with which others pursue the same thing. Adam Clarke reads it historically off the watches instituted at the rebuilding, where the men were divided so that those who worked by night rested by day, and so the beloved got sleep and rest. Matthew Henry presses the rebuke instead: it is part of our sentence to eat bread in the sweat of our face, but these go further, robbing their sleep to pay their cares.
3:
That children are a gift rather than a wage is pressed hardest by the two who look at the words. Keil and Delitzsch distinguish both nouns from what they resemble: the inheritance here is not one held by hereditary right but one given at the free will of the giver, and the reward is not a payment made in duty bound but a recompense bestowed by free judgment, looked for according to a promise given yet never to be demanded. Charles Ellicott makes the same point more briefly, that a heritage of the Lord is a heritage from him, a promise granted as the nation itself was a possession he made for himself. John Gill adds that the blessing is of good children, as the paraphrase interprets it. Adam Clarke turns it into a comparison of portions: to many God gives children in place of temporal good, and to others lands and gold with the womb that beareth not — and he asks where is the poor man who would give up his six children, with the prospect of more, for the millions of one who has neither root nor branch but his forlorn solitary self upon the earth. He adds the maxim that wherever God sends mouths he sends meat, and an eastern saying that a man should not murmur at a large family, since it is for their sakes that God feeds him.

Why the children of the youth are singled out gets three answers. Adam Clarke gives a physiological one: the children of young people are stronger, healthier and longer lived, youth being the time for marriage though not that comparative childhood in which several fools join in marriage who are scarcely fit to leave the nursery, while age produces only a dwarfish or rickety offspring; and having said it he draws back, remarking that it would be easy to assign reasons for all this but that the interpretation of Scripture will seldom admit of physiological details. John Wesley gives a domestic one, that such children live longest with their parents and to their support, where those born in old age seldom reach maturity before their parents die. Charles Ellicott gives a plain one, that it means the offspring of an early marriage, and cites an old translator who rendered it sons of young and vigorous parents.

What the full quiver is divides them at the close. John Gill takes it of the house full of children, the quiver being the case in which the arrows just mentioned are carried, and reports the versions which render it instead that the man’s desire is filled, having as many as he wishes for. Adam Clarke submits that it is more congenial to the metaphor to apply the quiver to the wife, so that the blessing is a fruitful wife rather than a full house, and defends the figure as Jewish in style and paralleled in a later book. The last clause is read as war by one and as law by another. Charles Ellicott notes that the persons who speak are not the sons but the parents, one of the sudden changes of number in which this poetry abounds, and argues that after the warrior and his arrows we should expect a martial image, so that they are not discomfited but challenge their enemies in the gates; yet he grants that the gate is so commonly the place where legal cases were decided that the other sense is natural. John Wesley takes it wholly of courts of judicature, where they plead their cause courageously without fear of being crushed by the might of their adversaries. Adam Clarke weighs both, observing that a man falsely accused has as many witnesses as he has children, but that one whose house is defended by vigorous sons need not fear marauders, and declares for the second.
